Lecture 7

Application I: molecular vibrations

This lecture counts the vibrational frequencies of the ammonia molecule and finds which of them are degenerate. It needs not a single force constant. We describe a molecule by the symmetry group of its equilibrium shape, its point group. The small oscillations about equilibrium are governed by the dynamical matrix, and the point group acts on the displacements of the atoms. The dynamical matrix commutes with that action, so Lecture 6’s block theorem applies: the vibrational frequencies fall into families labelled by irreducible representations, and characters count them. The lecture analyses the vibrations of ammonia in full, and the tutorial those of water.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Recognise the point groups CnvC_{nv}Cnv​ and DnhD_{nh}Dnh​ from a molecule’s shape.
  • Compute the displacement character and remove the rigid motions.
  • Classify the vibrations of a molecule by symmetry.

Molecules and their point groups

So far we have applied symmetry operations to triangles and polygons. Now we apply them to a real physical object — a molecule. No prior theory of molecules is needed: all we shall use is where the nuclei sit in space.

Picture a molecule as a few points in space. Each point is the nucleus of one atom at its equilibrium position, labelled by its species: the chemical element and, where it matters, the isotope. The water molecule H2_22​O, for instance, is three points: one oxygen and two hydrogens (Figure 7.1).

A symmetry operation of such a set of points is a rigid motion of space after which the molecule looks exactly the same. That means two things: the set of points is carried onto itself, and each nucleus is replaced by a nucleus of the same species. An oxygen nucleus may not land where a hydrogen was, and neither may a deuterium. Isotopes of one element feel the same forces but have different masses, and the masses enter the vibrations. The tutorial of Lecture 8 meets a molecule where this matters.

Definition 7.1 (Point group). The point group of a molecule is the group of all its symmetry operations under composition. The motions allowed are rotations, reflections and their combinations about the molecule’s centre of mass, that is, the orthogonal transformations.

The group is called a point group because all these operations keep one point fixed, the centre of mass. We take that point as the origin.

Chemists and physicists write these operations in Schoenflies notation:

  • EEE — the identity, that is, “do nothing”;

  • CnC_nCn​ — a rotation through 2π/n2\pi/n2π/n about some axis (the same symbol as the cyclic group this rotation generates);

  • σ\sigmaσ — a reflection in a plane.

The rotation axis of highest order is called the principal axis. A reflection plane gets the subscript vvv (vertical) if the principal axis lies in that plane. Planes that the group carries into one another share a name; planes that it does not are told apart by primes, σv\sigma_vσv​ and σv′\sigma_v'σv′​. The three vertical planes of ammonia, which its rotations carry into one another, are all σv\sigma_vσv​.

The name of a point group is built from the same symbols. For instance C2vC_{2v}C2v​ means that the principal axis is C2C_2C2​ and the reflection planes are vertical.

Finding the point group of a molecule is a search for these elements. For the molecules of this lecture and its sheet three questions settle it. Which is the principal axis CnC_nCn​? Are there nnn vertical planes through it? Is there also a plane perpendicular to it, called horizontal and written σh\sigma_hσh​? With nnn vertical planes and nothing more, the group is CnvC_{nv}Cnv​, of order 2n2n2n: water has n=2n=2n=2 and ammonia n=3n=3n=3. A horizontal plane as well brings nnn twofold axes perpendicular to the principal one, and the group is DnhD_{nh}Dnh​, of order 4n4n4n. Planar BF3_33​ (Sheet 7) has D3hD_{3h}D3h​. Other combinations give other groups.

The point group of ammonia is the group C3v≅S3C_{3v}\cong S_3C3v​≅S3​ whose character table Lecture 5 built; that of water is C2vC_{2v}C2v​, of order 444 (the tutorial).

The relabelling of nuclei [self-study]

Remark 7.2 (The relabelling the definition suppresses). Number the hydrogens of water H1_11​ and H2_22​. The rotation C2C_2C2​ interchanges them, so it does not leave the numbered molecule alone, although the molecule looks exactly the same. The definition asks only that each site be taken by a nucleus of the same species, not that each nucleus return to itself. Like nuclei are indistinguishable (Section 7.2), so we take the operation itself, an element of O(3)\Orth(3)O(3), as the group element, whatever the numbering. The permutation π(g)\pi(g)π(g) of the nuclei that ggg induces still does real work: the atoms ggg leaves in place are the fixed points of π(g)\pi(g)π(g), and Lemma 7.3 counts them.

Small oscillations and the dynamical matrix

Lecture 6’s block theorem needs an operator that commutes with the group. For a vibrating molecule that operator is the dynamical matrix, and this section builds it.

Consider a molecule of NNN atoms, labelled a=1,…,Na=1,\dots,Na=1,…,N, with masses mam_ama​. The origin OOO is the centre of mass (Section 7.1). Every point-group operation fixes it, so the operations act as linear maps. Write R⃗a 0∈R3\vec R_a^{\,0}\in\R^3Ra0​∈R3 for the position of atom aaa when the molecule rests at equilibrium. The superscript 000 is a label meaning “at equilibrium”, not a power. Write R⃗a∈R3\vec R_a\in\R^3Ra​∈R3 for the position of the same atom at some instant. The vector by which the atom has moved, u⃗a=R⃗a−R⃗a 0,equivalentlyR⃗a=R⃗a 0+u⃗a, \vec u_a=\vec R_a-\vec R_a^{\,0}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \vec R_a=\vec R_a^{\,0}+\vec u_a , ua​=Ra​−Ra0​,equivalentlyRa​=Ra0​+ua​,(7.1) is the displacement of atom aaa (Figure 7.2). These NNN small vectors are what the whole lecture is about.

The atoms interact through a potential VVV, a function of the instantaneous positions alone, and each nucleus obeys Newton’s law maR⃗¨a=−∇aV,a=1,…,N,m_a\ddot{\vec R}_a=-\nabla_aV, \qquad a=1,\dots,N,ma​R¨a​=−∇a​V,a=1,…,N, where ∇a\nabla_a∇a​ is the gradient with respect to R⃗a\vec R_aRa​ and a dot denotes a time derivative. This is our model of the molecule: point masses held together by the forces −∇aV-\nabla_aV−∇a​V. The light electrons enter only through VVV.

The molecule is isolated, so VVV depends on those positions only through the interatomic distances ∣R⃗a−R⃗b∣\big|\vec R_a-\vec R_b\big|​Ra​−Rb​​. So VVV is unchanged by every distance-preserving map of space applied to the whole molecule, reflections included. Nor does VVV change when two nuclei of the same species exchange places: they are indistinguishable, so VVV cannot tell which is which. Section 7.4 uses the first invariance, and Section 7.5 uses both.

The relation R⃗a=R⃗a 0+u⃗a\vec R_a=\vec R_a^{\,0}+\vec u_aRa​=Ra0​+ua​ lets us regard VVV as a function of the displacements. These are small, so VVV can be expanded in powers of them. Normal modes in full [self-study]

The real amplitude AkA_kAk​ and the phase φk\varphi_kφk​ in (7.4) are fixed by the initial conditions. Because the ε(k)\varepsilon^{(k)}ε(k) form a basis, the general solution of (7.3) is the superposition q(t)=∑k=13Nq(k)(t)q(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{3N}q^{(k)}(t)q(t)=k=1∑3N​q(k)(t) with one term per mode. For a zero mode the reduced equation is f¨=0\ddot f=0f¨​=0, so f(t)=Ak+Bktf(t)=A_k+B_ktf(t)=Ak​+Bk​t, and the motion is uniform rather than oscillatory. This is as it should be for the rigid motions of the molecule (Section 7.4).

Undoing the weighting in full gives the displacement an atom actually undergoes: uaα(t)=Akma εaα(k)cos⁡(ωkt+φk),u_{a\alpha}(t) =\frac{A_k}{\sqrt{m_a}}\,\varepsilon^{(k)}_{a\alpha} \cos\bigl(\omega_kt+\varphi_k\bigr),uaα​(t)=ma​​Ak​​εaα(k)​cos(ωk​t+φk​), so a heavy atom moves less than its component of ε(k)\varepsilon^{(k)}ε(k) would suggest. In water the oxygen is sixteen times heavier than a hydrogen, so the distinction matters in every mode.

At a stable equilibrium the potential has a minimum at u=0u=0u=0. So KKK, and with it DDD, is a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix: every ωk2≥0\omega_k^2\geq0ωk2​≥0.

The displacement representation

Next, the point group must act on the space where DDD acts. That is the 3N3N3N-dimensional real displacement space Vdisp=R3NV_{\mathrm{disp}}=\R^{3N}Vdisp​=R3N, whose vectors we read as displacements uuu, stacked as in (7.2), or, mass-weighted, as qqq. We write uau_aua​ for the three-vector block u⃗a\vec u_aua​ sitting at atom aaa, so a displacement is a vector-valued function on the set of atoms, a↦u⃗aa\mapsto\vec u_aa↦ua​.

Let GGG be the point group of the equilibrium configuration. We take it to be finite, since the character sums of Lecture 5 and the projectors of Lecture 6 are finite-group tools. Linear molecules, whose nuclei lie on one line and whose full point group is infinite, are therefore set aside. Section 7.4 notes only how their count of vibrations differs.

An operation g∈G⊂O(3)g\in G\subset\Orth(3)g∈G⊂O(3) does two things at once, and keeping them apart is the whole content of the construction. The operation ggg is an orthogonal map of space, with 3×33\times33×3 matrix R(g)R(g)R(g), so it rotates each displacement arrow. It also carries the equilibrium sites among themselves, R(g) R⃗a 0=R⃗g(a) 0, R(g)\,\vec R_a^{\,0}=\vec R_{g(a)}^{\,0}, R(g)Ra0​=Rg(a)0​,(7.5) that is, it permutes the atoms: g(a)g(a)g(a) is the label of the site that atom aaa is carried to. This label is well defined. The operation ggg is a symmetry, so the point R(g)R⃗a 0R(g)\vec R_a^{\,0}R(g)Ra0​ is again an equilibrium site, and a nucleus of the same species as atom aaa sits there. The matrix R(g)R(g)R(g) is invertible, so it carries distinct sites to distinct sites. The map a↦g(a)a\mapsto g(a)a↦g(a) is therefore a permutation of the labels 1,…,N1,\dots,N1,…,N.

For each operation ggg we define a linear operator ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) on the displacement space that carries the displacement field uuu along with the molecule. The transported field puts, at the new site, the rotated arrow from the old site: (ρ(g) u)g(a)=R(g) u⃗a,equivalently(ρ(g) u)a=R(g) u⃗ g−1(a). \bigl(\rho(g)\,u\bigr)_{g(a)}=R(g)\,\vec u_a, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \bigl(\rho(g)\,u\bigr)_{a}=R(g)\,\vec u_{\,g^{-1}(a)} . (ρ(g)u)g(a)​=R(g)ua​,equivalently(ρ(g)u)a​=R(g)ug−1(a)​.(7.6) The two forms say the same thing from opposite ends. The first follows an arrow forward to where it goes. The second asks what has arrived at site aaa and looks back to g−1(a)g^{-1}(a)g−1(a) to find it. The inverse is the familiar one from the function-space construction of Lecture 3. What is new is that the value is rotated as well as moved. The homomorphism property ρ(g)ρ(h)=ρ(gh)\rho(g)\rho(h)=\rho(gh)ρ(g)ρ(h)=ρ(gh) follows as in Lecture 3, now using R(g)R(h)=R(gh)R(g)R(h)=R(gh)R(g)R(h)=R(gh) as well. So ρ\rhoρ is a representation of GGG on VdispV_{\mathrm{disp}}Vdisp​, called the displacement representation. We write χdisp\chi_{\mathrm{disp}}χdisp​ for its character.

The same rule, with the same matrix, holds for the mass-weighted qqq, since ggg moves each nucleus to one of the same mass. The matrix of ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) is a permutation of 3×33\times33×3 blocks, each block the orthogonal R(g)R(g)R(g), so it is orthogonal.

To count the vibrations, all we need from this representation is its character. The fixed-point lemma of Lecture 5, extended by the 3×33\times33×3 trace, gives it at once. Besides rotations and reflections, Lemma 7.3 below covers two more kinds of operation. The inversion iii through the centre is x⃗↦−x⃗\vec x\mapsto-\vec xx↦−x. The rotoreflection S(θ)S(\theta)S(θ) is a rotation through θ\thetaθ followed by the reflection in the plane perpendicular to its axis. Discarding rigid motions

Six of the 3N3N3N degrees of freedom are not vibrations. A rigid translation, u⃗a=t⃗\vec u_a=\vec tua​=t for all aaa, moves no atom relative to any other. An infinitesimal rotation, u⃗a=δω⃗×R⃗a 0\vec u_a=\delta\vec\omega\times\vec R_a^{\,0}ua​=δω×Ra0​, with δω⃗\delta\vec\omegaδω along the axis and as long as the small angle turned, is the first-order part of a rigid rotation: each atom moves perpendicular to its position vector (Figure 7.3). It changes the interatomic distances, but only at second order.

Both are zero modes. Write www for either motion, w⃗a=t⃗\vec w_a=\vec twa​=t or w⃗a=δω⃗×R⃗a 0\vec w_a=\delta\vec\omega\times\vec R_a^{\,0}wa​=δω×Ra0​, stacked like uuu. The potential VVV is constant along a rigid motion, so its second derivative along the motion vanishes. At equilibrium that second derivative is wTKww^{\mathsf T}KwwTKw (for the rotation this takes a short argument, given in self-study below), so wTKw=0w^{\mathsf T}Kw=0wTKw=0. At a minimum KKK is positive semidefinite, and then Kw=0Kw=0Kw=0: in an orthonormal eigenbasis of KKK, with eigenvalues λj≥0\lambda_j\geq0λj​≥0 and coordinates cjc_jcj​ of www, the sum wTKw=∑jλjcj2w^{\mathsf T}Kw=\sum_j\lambda_jc_j^2wTKw=∑j​λj​cj2​ vanishes only if every λjcj=0\lambda_jc_j=0λj​cj​=0.

In detail, take the genuine rigid path R⃗a(s)=Q(s)R⃗a 0\vec R_a(s)=Q(s)\vec R_a^{\,0}Ra​(s)=Q(s)Ra0​ with Q(s)Q(s)Q(s) a rotation, Q(0)=1Q(0)=\IdQ(0)=1. The picture follows one atom: the path is an arc, and the tangent s w⃗as\,\vec w_aswa​ departs from it only by O(s2)O(s^2)O(s2).

Its displacements are u⃗a(s)=Q(s)R⃗a 0−R⃗a 0\vec u_a(s)=Q(s)\vec R_a^{\,0}-\vec R_a^{\,0}ua​(s)=Q(s)Ra0​−Ra0​, with u(0)=0u(0)=0u(0)=0. Symmetry block-diagonalises DDD

The group GGG is a symmetry of the molecule, so the potential VVV does not change when ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) acts on the displacements. To see this, look at where the atoms end up. In the displaced configuration ρ(g)u\rho(g)uρ(g)u, the atom at site aaa sits at R⃗a 0+(ρ(g)u)a=R(g)(R⃗g−1(a) 0+u⃗ g−1(a))=R(g) R⃗g−1(a),\vec R_a^{\,0}+\bigl(\rho(g)u\bigr)_a =R(g)\bigl(\vec R_{g^{-1}(a)}^{\,0}+\vec u_{\,g^{-1}(a)}\bigr) =R(g)\,\vec R_{g^{-1}(a)},Ra0​+(ρ(g)u)a​=R(g)(Rg−1(a)0​+ug−1(a)​)=R(g)Rg−1(a)​, by (7.5) and (7.6). This is the old configuration, rotated by R(g)R(g)R(g), with like nuclei renumbered. Neither the rotation nor the renumbering changes VVV (Section 7.2). So V(ρ(g)u)=V(u)V\bigl(\rho(g)u\bigr)=V(u)V(ρ(g)u)=V(u) for all g∈Gg\in Gg∈G and all displacements. For the harmonic potential V=V(0)+12 uTKu=V(0)+12 qTDqV=V(0)+\frac12\,u^{\mathsf T}Ku=V(0)+\frac12\,q^{\mathsf T}DqV=V(0)+21​uTKu=V(0)+21​qTDq this reads ρ(g)TD ρ(g)=D\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}D\,\rho(g)=Dρ(g)TDρ(g)=D. The matrices ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) are orthogonal, so [D, ρ(g)]=0for all g∈G. \bigl[D,\,\rho(g)\bigr]=0 \qquad\text{for all }g\in G . [D,ρ(g)]=0for all g∈G.(7.7) So the dynamical matrix plays the part of Lecture 6’s Hamiltonian. That lecture’s block theorem asks for two things, both now in hand. The group acts on VvibV_{\mathrm{vib}}Vvib​ by orthogonal, hence unitary, matrices (Sections 7.3 and 7.4). And DDD maps VvibV_{\mathrm{vib}}Vvib​ into itself, because the image of a symmetric matrix is orthogonal to its kernel. On VvibV_{\mathrm{vib}}Vvib​ the matrix DDD is a real symmetric operator that commutes with every ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g). Characters and projectors work over C\CC, so we let the same real matrices act on complex combinations q1+iq2q_1+\ii q_2q1​+iq2​ with q1,q2∈Vvibq_1,q_2\in V_{\mathrm{vib}}q1​,q2​∈Vvib​; the physical displacements are the real ones. Decompose Vvib≅⨁imi V(i).V_{\mathrm{vib}}\cong\bigoplus_i m_i\,V^{(i)}.Vvib​≅i⨁​mi​V(i). In a symmetry-adapted basis, DDD acts on each isotypic component through an mi×mim_i\times m_imi​×mi​ reduced matrix F(i)F^{(i)}F(i), the same for every partner index. The squared frequencies ω2\omega^2ω2 are the eigenvalues of the F(i)F^{(i)}F(i), each with at least ni=dim⁡V(i)n_i=\dim V^{(i)}ni​=dimV(i) independent modes of one symmetry type. A type that occurs once (mi=1m_i=1mi​=1) gives normal modes by symmetry alone. The molecules of this lecture have real characters, so their projectors are real matrices, and the adapted vectors and the modes can be taken real. Group theory fixes the block structure; the spring constants and masses only fill in the small matrices F(i)F^{(i)}F(i).

[self-study]

A degeneracy larger than nin_ini​ is accidental, or it comes from reality: the displacements are real, so irreducibles with non-real characters pair up (Lecture 6).

The practical recipe, then:

  1. identify the point group GGG of the equilibrium configuration;

  2. compute χdisp(g)=Ng χvec(g)\chi_{\mathrm{disp}}(g)=N_g\,\chi_{\mathrm{vec}}(g)χdisp​(g)=Ng​χvec​(g) class by class;

  3. subtract χtrans\chi_{\mathrm{trans}}χtrans​ and χrot\chi_{\mathrm{rot}}χrot​;

  4. extract multiplicities mi=⟨χi,χvib⟩Gm_i=\inner{\chi_i}{\chi_{\mathrm{vib}}}_Gmi​=⟨χi​,χvib​⟩G​ from the character table;

  5. construct symmetry-adapted coordinates with the projectors of Lecture 6, and diagonalise each reduced F(i)F^{(i)}F(i) that is larger than 1×11\times11×1.

Worked example: ammonia

Ammonia is a triangular pyramid of N=4N=4N=4 atoms. We find its point group by answering the three questions of Section 7.1. The principal axis is a C3C_3C3​ through the nitrogen. Three vertical planes pass through it, each through the nitrogen and one hydrogen. There is no horizontal plane, since the nitrogen lies off the plane of the hydrogens. So the group is C3vC_{3v}C3v​. Its character table was built in Lecture 5. The classes have sizes 1,2,31,2,31,2,3, and the character bookkeeping is E2C33σvNg412χvec301χdisp1202χtrans301χrot30−1χvib602χA1111χA211−1χE2−10\def\arraystretch{1.2} \begin{array}{l|ccc} & E & 2C_3 & 3\sigma_v\\ \hline N_g & 4 & 1 & 2\\ \chi_{\mathrm{vec}} & 3 & 0 & 1\\ \chi_{\mathrm{disp}} & 12 & 0 & 2\\ \chi_{\mathrm{trans}} & 3 & 0 & 1\\ \chi_{\mathrm{rot}} & 3 & 0 & -1\\ \hline \chi_{\mathrm{vib}} & 6 & 0 & 2\\ \hline \chi_{A_1} & 1 & 1 & 1\\ \chi_{A_2} & 1 & 1 & -1\\ \chi_{E} & 2 & -1 & 0 \end{array}Ng​χvec​χdisp​χtrans​χrot​χvib​χA1​​χA2​​χE​​E4312336112​2C3​10000011−1​3σv​2121−121−10​​ It remains to find how often each irreducible representation occurs in VvibV_{\mathrm{vib}}Vvib​. These are six vibrational dimensions (3N−6=63N-6=63N−6=6 ). Generically, that is barring the accidents that Lecture 6’s corollary on symmetry-enforced degeneracy leaves open, there are four distinct frequencies: two nondegenerate A1A_1A1​ frequencies and two doubly degenerate EEE frequencies. The double degeneracies are not accidents of a particular model of the forces. They are theorems.

For explicit modes, internal coordinates serve best (Figure 7.1, right): the three bond stretches sks_ksk​, the increase in length of the bond N–Hk_kk​, and the three angle changes δk\delta_kδk​, the increase of the H–N–H angle opposite Hk_kk​. These are six coordinates for six vibrations. Each is, to first order, a linear function of qqq, and we use the same letter for its vector: sk(q)=skTqs_k(q)=s_k^{\mathsf T}qsk​(q)=skT​q, and likewise for δk\delta_kδk​. An operation ggg that takes Hk_kk​ to Hg(k)_{g(k)}g(k)​ carries bond kkk to bond g(k)g(k)g(k), and the angle opposite Hk_kk​ to the angle opposite Hg(k)_{g(k)}g(k)​, so ρ(g) sk=sg(k),ρ(g) δk=δg(k).\rho(g)\,s_k=s_{g(k)}, \qquad \rho(g)\,\delta_k=\delta_{g(k)} .ρ(g)sk​=sg(k)​,ρ(g)δk​=δg(k)​. So the group permutes the six vectors, and they are what we project. For ammonia they form a basis of VvibV_{\mathrm{vib}}Vvib​ (self-study below).

Here we used that none of the coordinates changes under a rigid motion, so each vector is orthogonal to the rigid motions and lies in VvibV_{\mathrm{vib}}Vvib​; for ammonia the six are independent. Moreover, the displacement ρ(g)q\rho(g)qρ(g)q stretches bond g(k)g(k)g(k) as qqq stretches bond kkk, so sg(k)Tρ(g)q=skTqs_{g(k)}^{\mathsf T}\rho(g)q=s_k^{\mathsf T}qsg(k)T​ρ(g)q=skT​q for every qqq. Hence ρ(g)Tsg(k)=sk\rho(g)^{\mathsf T}s_{g(k)}=s_kρ(g)Tsg(k)​=sk​, and ρ(g)\rho(g)ρ(g) is orthogonal, so ρ(g)sk=sg(k)\rho(g)s_k=s_{g(k)}ρ(g)sk​=sg(k)​.

The rotations cycle the indices, and the reflection in the plane through H1_11​ swaps 2↔32\leftrightarrow32↔3, for the sks_ksk​ and the δk\delta_kδk​ alike. Each triple therefore carries the permutation representation of S3S_3S3​, which decomposes as A1⊕EA_1\oplus EA1​⊕E (Lecture 6’s example of the projectors on the triangle’s orbitals), and Γvib=(A1⊕E)stretch⊕(A1⊕E)bend,\Gamma_{\mathrm{vib}} =(A_1\oplus E)_{\text{stretch}}\oplus(A_1\oplus E)_{\text{bend}},Γvib​=(A1​⊕E)stretch​⊕(A1​⊕E)bend​, in agreement with the Cartesian count. The projectors are exactly those of that example: PA1=J/3P_{A_1}=J/3PA1​​=J/3 and PE=1−J/3P_E=\Id-J/3PE​=1−J/3 on each triple, with JJJ the 3×33\times33×3 matrix of ones. Applied to s1s_1s1​ and to δ1\delta_1δ1​, the projector PA1P_{A_1}PA1​​ gives the two A1A_1A1​ coordinates, up to a factor 13\tfrac1331​: s1+s2+s3⏟symmetric stretch (A1),δ1+δ2+δ3⏟umbrella (A1).\underbrace{s_1+s_2+s_3}_{\text{symmetric stretch }(A_1)}, \qquad \underbrace{\delta_1+\delta_2+\delta_3} _{\text{umbrella }(A_1)}.symmetric stretch (A1​)s1​+s2​+s3​​​,umbrella (A1​)δ1​+δ2​+δ3​​​. In the symmetric stretch the three bonds lengthen together. In the umbrella the three angles open together: the pyramid flattens, and the nitrogen moves along the axis against the hydrogens (Figure 7.4).

From each triple PEP_EPE​ gives a pair of EEE partners. For the stretches, PE s1=13 (2s1−s2−s3),PE (s2−s3)=s2−s3,P_E\,s_1=\frac13\,(2s_1-s_2-s_3), \qquad P_E\,(s_2-s_3)=s_2-s_3,PE​s1​=31​(2s1​−s2​−s3​),PE​(s2​−s3​)=s2​−s3​, the asymmetric-stretch pair, and the same with δk\delta_kδk​ in place of sks_ksk​ gives the asymmetric-bend pair. Symmetry alone does not make these normal modes. The two A1A_1A1​ coordinates generically mix through a 2×22\times22×2 reduced matrix. So do the two EEE pairs, with one 2×22\times22×2 matrix for both partners, because the two pairs are built alike. With the six zero modes set aside, a 12×1212\times1212×12 eigenvalue problem has become two 2×22\times22×2 problems.

The measured spectrum agrees. Ammonia shows four fundamental frequencies, absorption lines at the mode frequencies ωk\omega_kωk​ themselves rather than at their sums or multiples. They are quoted as wavenumbers ν~=ω/2πc\tilde\nu=\omega/2\pi cν~=ω/2πc, with ccc the speed of light (NIST, after Shimanouchi): modetypeν~ (cm−1)symmetric stretchA13337umbrellaA1950asymmetric stretchE3444asymmetric bendE1627\def\arraystretch{1.2} \begin{array}{lcc} \text{mode} & \text{type} & \tilde\nu\ (\mathrm{cm}^{-1})\\ \hline \text{symmetric stretch} & A_1 & 3337\\ \text{umbrella} & A_1 & 950\\ \text{asymmetric stretch} & E & 3444\\ \text{asymmetric bend} & E & 1627 \end{array}modesymmetric stretchumbrellaasymmetric stretchasymmetric bend​typeA1​A1​EE​ν~ (cm−1)333795034441627​​ Modes of one type mix, so each name records the internal coordinate that dominates the mode. Which of these vibrations infrared light can excite is a further question, answered in Lecture 8.

The umbrella line is in fact split in two, because the nitrogen can tunnel through the plane of the hydrogens. That effect lies outside the harmonic picture.

[self-study]

Internal coordinates: a caveat. For water and ammonia the natural internal coordinates are exactly 3N−63N-63N−6 independent ones, so the bookkeeping closes. In general they must be checked on two counts. They can be redundant: around a ring, or around an atom with many neighbours, the angles obey relations. And they can be incomplete. In planar BF3_33​ (Sheet 7) the three stretches and the three bond angles carry 2A1′⊕2E′2A_1'\oplus2E'2A1′​⊕2E′, whereas the vibrations are A1′⊕2E′⊕A2′′A_1'\oplus2E'\oplus A_2''A1′​⊕2E′⊕A2′′​ (one prime marks a type even under σh\sigma_hσh​, two primes a type odd under it). The three angles always add up to 2π2\pi2π, which costs an A1′A_1'A1′​, and no bond length or angle sees the umbrella motion out of the plane, which is the A2′′A_2''A2′′​. The Cartesian route of Sections 7.3–7.4 is never ambiguous.

Worked example: water [tutorial]

Water is bent: N=3N=3N=3, point group C2v={E,C2,σv,σv′}C_{2v}=\{E,C_2,\sigma_v,\sigma_v'\}C2v​={E,C2​,σv​,σv′​} (Section 7.1): the half-turn C2C_2C2​ about the axis that bisects the H–O–H angle, and the reflections in two planes through that axis. Every operation squares to EEE, and composing two distinct nonidentity operations gives the third. So C2vC_{2v}C2v​ is not cyclic: it is the Klein four-group named in Lecture 1. We place the molecule in the yzyzyz-plane with the C2C_2C2​ axis along zzz. Let σv\sigma_vσv​ denote the molecular plane (yzyzyz) and σv′\sigma_v'σv′​ the perpendicular plane (xzxzxz). The group is abelian of order 444, so its four irreducible characters are one-dimensional sign characters. With Mulliken labels they are C2vEC2σv(yz)σv′(xz)A11111zA211−1−1B11−11−1yB21−1−11x\def\arraystretch{1.2} \begin{array}{c|cccc|l} C_{2v} & E & C_2 & \sigma_v(yz) & \sigma_v'(xz) & \\ \hline A_1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & z\\ A_2 & 1 & 1 & -1 & -1 & \\ B_1 & 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 & y\\ B_2 & 1 & -1 & -1 & 1 & x \end{array}C2v​A1​A2​B1​B2​​E1111​C2​11−1−1​σv​(yz)1−11−1​σv′​(xz)1−1−11​zyx​​ The last column records how the coordinate functions transform, which we need shortly. Note that interchanging the two planes interchanges the labels B1↔B2B_1\leftrightarrow B_2B1​↔B2​. Conventions differ between books, so fix one and stay consistent. Most tables, NIST’s among them, also put water in the yzyzyz-plane but attach B1B_1B1​ to the other plane, xzxzxz. There water’s antisymmetric stretch is B2B_2B2​; here it is B1B_1B1​.

Step 1: characters. The numbers of atoms left in place and the traces are EC2σv(yz)σv′(xz)Ng3131χvec3−111χdisp=Ngχvec9−131χtrans3−111χrot=det⁡⋅χvec3−1−1−1χvib3131\def\arraystretch{1.2} \begin{array}{l|cccc} & E & C_2 & \sigma_v(yz) & \sigma_v'(xz)\\ \hline N_g & 3 & 1 & 3 & 1\\ \chi_{\mathrm{vec}} & 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\\ \chi_{\mathrm{disp}}=N_g\chi_{\mathrm{vec}} & 9 & -1 & 3 & 1\\ \chi_{\mathrm{trans}} & 3 & -1 & 1 & 1\\ \chi_{\mathrm{rot}}=\det\cdot\chi_{\mathrm{vec}} & 3 & -1 & -1 & -1\\ \hline \chi_{\mathrm{vib}} & 3 & 1 & 3 & 1 \end{array}Ng​χvec​χdisp​=Ng​χvec​χtrans​χrot​=det⋅χvec​χvib​​E339333​C2​1−1−1−1−11​σv​(yz)3131−13​σv′​(xz)1111−11​​ Here NC2=1N_{C_2}=1NC2​​=1 because only the oxygen sits on the axis, Nσv=3N_{\sigma_v}=3Nσv​​=3 because the whole molecule lies in its own plane, and Nσv′=1N_{\sigma_v'}=1Nσv′​​=1 because only the oxygen lies in the perpendicular plane.

Step 2: multiplicities. All class sizes are 111 and ∣G∣=4\abs G=4∣G∣=4, so mA1=14(3+1+3+1)=2,mA2=14(3+1−3−1)=0,mB1=14(3−1+3−1)=1,mB2=14(3−1−3+1)=0,\begin{align*} m_{A_1}&=\frac14(3+1+3+1)=2, & m_{A_2}&=\frac14(3+1-3-1)=0,\\ m_{B_1}&=\frac14(3-1+3-1)=1, & m_{B_2}&=\frac14(3-1-3+1)=0, \end{align*}mA1​​mB1​​​=41​(3+1+3+1)=2,=41​(3−1+3−1)=1,​mA2​​mB2​​​=41​(3+1−3−1)=0,=41​(3−1−3+1)=0,​ so Γvib=2A1⊕B1,\Gamma_{\mathrm{vib}}=2A_1\oplus B_1,Γvib​=2A1​⊕B1​, that is, three vibrational coordinates (3N−6=33N-6=33N−6=3 ). Two of them have the full symmetry A1A_1A1​, and one is antisymmetric under both C2C_2C2​ and σv′\sigma_v'σv′​. Generically the 2×22\times22×2 reduced A1A_1A1​ block has two distinct eigenvalues, neither equal to the B1B_1B1​ one, so all three frequencies are distinct. Any coincidence, inside the block or across the blocks, would be accidental.

Step 3: symmetry-adapted coordinates by projection. What the projectors return is a basis adapted to the symmetry, not eigenvectors of DDD. Symmetry guarantees that a projected vector is a normal mode only when its symmetry type occurs once. Where an irreducible occurs mi>1m_i>1mi​>1 times, the reduced matrix F(i)F^{(i)}F(i) generically mixes the copies, and the modes follow only after F(i)F^{(i)}F(i) is diagonalised.

As for ammonia, the vibrational physics is most transparent in internal coordinates. For water they are the two bond stretches s1,s2s_1,s_2s1​,s2​ (elongations of the O–H bonds) and the bend δ\deltaδ (the increase of the H–O–H angle): three coordinates for three vibrations. The group permutes them simply. The operations C2C_2C2​ and σv′\sigma_v'σv′​ swap s1↔s2s_1\leftrightarrow s_2s1​↔s2​, while EEE and σv\sigma_vσv​ fix each. The bend δ\deltaδ is invariant under everything, so it is pure A1A_1A1​. Applying the projectors of Lecture 6 to the trial vector s1s_1s1​ gives PA1s1=14(s1+s2+s1+s2)=12(s1+s2),PB1s1=14(s1+(−1)s2+s1+(−1)s2)=12(s1−s2),\begin{align*} P_{A_1}s_1&=\frac14\bigl(s_1+s_2+s_1+s_2\bigr) =\frac12(s_1+s_2),\\ P_{B_1}s_1&=\frac14\bigl(s_1+(-1)s_2+s_1+(-1)s_2\bigr) =\frac12(s_1-s_2), \end{align*}PA1​​s1​PB1​​s1​​=41​(s1​+s2​+s1​+s2​)=21​(s1​+s2​),=41​(s1​+(−1)s2​+s1​+(−1)s2​)=21​(s1​−s2​),​ with PA2s1=PB2s1=0P_{A_2}s_1=P_{B_2}s_1=0PA2​​s1​=PB2​​s1​=0. So the three symmetry-adapted vibrations of water are (Figure 7.5) s1+s2⏟symmetric stretch (A1),δ⏟bend (A1),s1−s2⏟antisymmetric stretch (B1).\underbrace{s_1+s_2}_{\text{symmetric stretch }(A_1)}, \qquad \underbrace{\delta}_{\text{bend }(A_1)}, \qquad \underbrace{s_1-s_2}_{\text{antisymmetric stretch }(B_1)}.symmetric stretch (A1​)s1​+s2​​​,bend (A1​)δ​​,antisymmetric stretch (B1​)s1​−s2​​​.

Lecture 6’s block theorem adds a final refinement that pictures of modes do not show. The two A1A_1A1​ coordinates span a single isotypic component with mA1=2m_{A_1}=2mA1​​=2. So symmetry does not make the symmetric stretch and the bend normal modes. Generically the actual eigenvectors are two combinations of them, orthogonal in the mass-weighted coordinates qqq and determined by the 2×22\times22×2 reduced matrix F(A1)F^{(A_1)}F(A1​), whose entries depend on the force constants. The B1B_1B1​ mode is alone in its symmetry type, so it is an exact normal mode by symmetry alone. Group theory has reduced a 9×99\times99×9 problem to a 2×22\times22×2 problem (A1A_1A1​), a 1×11\times11×1 problem (B1B_1B1​), and the six rigid modes already known to have zero frequency.

Summary

  • Point groups. A molecule’s symmetry operations form its point group; ammonia’s is C3v≅S3C_{3v}\cong S_3C3v​≅S3​, water’s C2vC_{2v}C2v​.
  • Vibrations as a representation. Nuclear displacements carry a (generally reducible) representation of the molecule’s point group (eq. (7.6)).
  • Mode counting. The displacement character is read off the atoms a symmetry leaves in place (Lemma 7.3). Removing the translations and rotations (Lemma 7.4) leaves the vibrational content, 3N−63N-63N−6 dimensions for a nonlinear molecule.
  • Symmetry commutes. The point group commutes with the dynamical matrix (eq. (7.7)), so Lecture 6’s block theorem applies: frequencies are labelled by irreducibles, each at least dim⁡V(i)\dim V^{(i)}dimV(i)-fold degenerate.
  • Ammonia. Γvib=2A1⊕2E\Gamma_{\mathrm{vib}}=2A_1\oplus2EΓvib​=2A1​⊕2E: generically four frequencies, two of them doubly degenerate, before any force constant is known, and four are measured. The projectors of Lecture 6 give the symmetry-adapted coordinates; symmetry guarantees that they are normal modes only where a type occurs once.

Self-check

5 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes.

1In the displacement character, which atoms contribute to the trace of a symmetry operation?

Here is the hint — try once more.Moved atoms occupy off-diagonal permutation blocks.Only fixed atoms contribute diagonal blocks and hence trace.

2How many vibrational normal modes does nonlinear H₂O have?

Use 3N−6 for a nonlinear molecule, with N=3.

Here is the hint — try once more.3×3−6=3: two stretches and a bend.

3Which C₂ᵥ symmetry type contains the symmetric O–H stretch of water?

Here is the hint — try once more.It is left unchanged by every molecular symmetry operation.The fully symmetric coordinate transforms as A₁.

4Does the H–O–H bend have the same symmetry type as the symmetric stretch?

Here is the hint — try once more.Both hydrogens move symmetrically.Both normal coordinates transform as A₁, though the dynamical matrix gives them different frequencies.

5What happens to the antisymmetric stretch when the two hydrogens are exchanged?

Here is the hint — try once more.One bond lengthens while the other shortens.Exchange reverses this coordinate, which is what distinguishes its B₁ type.
